results.title: Odd greedy choice
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a rational number $r$ and a natural number $d$, $d$ is the odd greedy choice at $r$ when $r > 0$, $d$ is positive and odd, $1/d \le r$, and $d \le e$ for every positive odd natural number $e$ with $1/e \le r$. Equivalently, $1/d$ is the largest unit fraction with odd denominator that does not exceed $r$.

results.title: The odd greedy choice needs a positive remainder
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $d$ is the odd greedy choice at a rational number $r$, then $r > 0$.

results.title: The odd greedy choice is positive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $d$ is the odd greedy choice at a rational number $r$, then $d > 0$.

results.title: The odd greedy choice is odd
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $d$ is the odd greedy choice at a rational number $r$, then $d$ is odd.

results.title: The odd greedy unit fraction does not exceed the remainder
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $d$ is the odd greedy choice at a rational number $r$, then $1/d \le r$.

results.title: The odd greedy choice is minimal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $d$ is the odd greedy choice at a rational number $r$, then $d \le e$ for every positive odd natural number $e$ with $1/e \le r$.

results.title: Uniqueness of the odd greedy choice
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $d$ and $d'$ are both odd greedy choices at the same rational number $r$, then $d = d'$.

results.title: Characterization of the odd greedy choice
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A natural number $d$ is the odd greedy choice at a rational number $r$ if and only if $r > 0$ and $d$ is the least element of the set of positive odd natural numbers $e$ with $1/e \le r$.

results.title: Even sums of odd unit fractions have even numerator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be an even natural number and let $d_1, \dots, d_m$ be odd natural numbers. If integers $a$ and $b$ with $b \ne 0$ satisfy $a/b = \sum_{i=1}^{m} 1/d_i$, then $a$ is even.

results.title: Odd greedy choice at a fraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ and $d$ be positive natural numbers and let $x_1$ be an odd natural number. Then $x_1$ is the odd greedy choice at $n/d$ (the first denominator of the odd greedy expansion of $n/d$) if and only if $d \le n x_1$ and $n x_1 < d + 2n$, that is, $0 \le n x_1 - d < 2n$ in the integers.

results.title: Bonferroni rejection set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The hypotheses rejected by the Bonferroni procedure at level `α`: those whose p-value is at most `α / m`.

results.title: Union bound for valid p-values
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If every true-null p-value is valid and `c ∈ [0, 1]`, the probability that some true null has p-value at most `c` is at most `|H0| c`. No independence is assumed.

results.title: Bonferroni inequality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If every true-null p-value is valid, the probability that some true null has p-value at most `α / m` is at most `α |H0| / m`, for `α ∈ [0, 1]`. No independence is assumed. (For `m = 0` there is no hypothesis and both sides are `0`.)

results.title: The Bonferroni procedure controls the FWER
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If every true-null p-value is valid, the probability that the Bonferroni procedure at level `α ∈ [0, 1]` rejects at least one true null is at most `α`.

results.title: Ramsey graphs for the triangle
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A graph $G$ on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ is $r$-Ramsey for the triangle when every colouring $c$ of the ordered pairs of vertices with $r$ colours that is symmetric ($c(a, b) = c(b, a)$) admits three distinct vertices $u, v, w$ that form a triangle in $G$ with $c(u, v) = c(v, w) = c(w, u)$.

results.title: Instances of PRECOLORING EXTENSION
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of precoloring extension is a tuple $(n, E, c, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges), a list $c$ of natural numbers (the partial coloring, where an entry $0$ means uncolored and an entry $k + 1$ means color $k$), and a natural number $K$ (the number of colors).

results.title: Well-formed precoloring extension instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, c, K)$ of precoloring extension is well formed when the edge list $E$ has no repeated entries, every edge $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$, and the partial coloring $c$ has length $n$.

results.title: Feasible precoloring extension instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, E, c, K)$ of precoloring extension is feasible when there is a list $\chi = (\chi_0, \dots, \chi_{n-1})$ of $n$ natural numbers such that $\chi_v < K$ for every vertex $v < n$, $\chi_v = c_v - 1$ for every vertex $v < n$ with $c_v \ne 0$, and $\chi_u \ne \chi_v$ for every edge $(u, v)$ in $E$. Here $c_v$ is the entry of $c$ at position $v$, and an entry of a list at a position beyond its length is…

results.title: PRECOLORING EXTENSION as a decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem PRECOLORING EXTENSION accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a precoloring extension instance that is well formed and feasible; bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

results.title: PRECOLORING EXTENSION is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem PRECOLORING EXTENSION lies in NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

results.title: Preimage of a set under a letter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a set $C$ of states and a letter $a$, the preimage of $C$ under $a$ is the set of states $q$ with $\delta(q, a) \in C$.

results.title: A set of states split by another
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A set $D$ of states is split by a set $P$ of states when $D$ contains both a state in $P$ and a state not in $P$, that is, when $D \cap P$ and $D \setminus P$ are both nonempty.

results.title: Splitting a block by a set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For sets $P$ and $D$ of states, splitting $D$ by $P$ gives the two-element list $[D \cap P,\ D \setminus P]$ if both of these sets are nonempty, and the one-element list $[D]$ otherwise.

results.title: Smaller of two finite sets of states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For finite sets $A$ and $B$ of states, the smaller one is $A$ if $|A| \le |B|$ and $B$ otherwise; on a tie in cardinality it is $A$.

results.title: One refinement round of the partition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a list $P$ of blocks of states, a set $C$ of states and a letter $a$, let $S = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$ be the preimage of $C$ under $a$. The partition after the splitter $(C, a)$ replaces each block $D$ of $P$, in order, by the two blocks $D \cap S$ and $D \setminus S$ when both are nonempty, and keeps $D$ otherwise.

The waiting list after the splitter $(C, a)$, from the rest $W$ of the waiting list, consists of…

results.title: Block of accepting states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ with finite state set $Q$, this is the set $F \subseteq Q$ of accepting states of $M$, as a finite set.

results.title: Rejecting states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ with state set $Q$ and set of accepting states $F$, the rejecting block is the set $Q \setminus F$ of states of $M$ that are not accepting.

results.title: Hopcroft's initial partition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ with finite state set $Q$ and set of accepting states $F$, the initial partition is the list of blocks $F$, $Q \setminus F$, in this order, with any empty block removed.

results.title: Hopcroft's initial waiting list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$, set of accepting states $F$ and finite alphabet $\Sigma$. If $F$ and $Q \setminus F$ are both nonempty, the initial waiting list consists of the splitters $(S, b)$ for every letter $b \in \Sigma$, where $S = F$ if $|F| \le |Q \setminus F|$ and $S = Q \setminus F$ otherwise; if one of $F$ and $Q \setminus F$ is empty, the initial waiting list is empty.

results.title: Hopcroft's refinement loop
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA. Given a round budget $k$, a partition $P$ of the states of $M$ (a list of blocks) and a waiting list $W$ of splitters $(C, a)$, each a block $C$ with a letter $a$, the loop returns the pair $(P, W)$ unchanged if $k = 0$ or $W$ is empty. Otherwise it removes the first splitter $(C, a)$ from $W$, replaces $P$ by the partition after the splitter $(C, a)$ and the remaining waiting list by the waiting…

results.title: Hopcroft's partition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$. Hopcroft's partition of $M$ is the partition returned by Hopcroft's loop run from the initial partition and the initial waiting list with a budget of $|\Sigma| \cdot (|Q| + 1)$ rounds.

results.title: Hopcroft's relation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ with finitely many states, Hopcroft's relation is the set of pairs $(p, q)$ of states of $M$ such that $p$ and $q$ lie in a common block of Hopcroft's partition.

results.title: Partitions of the states
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A list $P$ of sets of states is a partition into nonempty blocks when entries of $P$ at different positions are disjoint, every entry of $P$ is nonempty, and every state lies in some entry of $P$.

results.title: Lying in a common block
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $P$ of sets of states, two states $p$ and $q$ are related by $P$ when some block $D$ of $P$ contains both $p$ and $q$.

results.title: A block contains both or neither of two related states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a list of sets of states that is a partition into nonempty blocks, let $C$ be an entry of $P$, and let $p$ and $q$ be states lying in a common entry of $P$. Then $p \in C$ if and only if $q \in C$.

results.title: A partition has at most as many blocks as there are states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a list $P$ of sets of states is a partition into nonempty blocks, then the length of $P$ is at most the number $|Q|$ of states.

results.title: Pieces of a split block lie on one side
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ and $D$ be sets of states. Every piece of $D$ split by $S$ (the two sets $D \cap S$ and $D \setminus S$ if $D$ meets both $S$ and its complement, and $D$ itself otherwise) is contained in $S$ or disjoint from $S$: any two states $x$ and $y$ of the piece satisfy $x \in S \iff y \in S$.

results.title: Effect of one splitter on the common-block relation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$, $P$ a list of blocks of states, $C$ a set of states and $a$ a letter. Two states $p$ and $q$ lie in a common block after the splitter $(C, a)$ is applied to $P$ if and only if they lie in a common block of $P$ and $\delta(p, a) \in C \iff \delta(q, a) \in C$.

results.title: Number of blocks after one round
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$, let $P$ be a list of sets of states, $C$ a set of states and $a$ a letter, and let $\mathrm{pre} = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$. The partition after the splitter $(C, a)$, which replaces each entry $D$ of $P$ meeting both $\mathrm{pre}$ and its complement by $D \cap \mathrm{pre}$ and $D \setminus \mathrm{pre}$, has length equal to the length of $P$ plus the number…

results.title: Growth of the waiting list in one round
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, let $P$ be a list of sets of states with no repeated entries, let $W$ be a list of pairs of a set of states and a letter, let $C$ be a set of states and $a$ a letter, and let $S = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$ be the preimage of $C$ under $a$. Then the waiting list after the splitter $(C, a)$, computed from the blocks $P$ and the rest…

results.title: Invariants of Hopcroft's loop
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$. A list $P$ of sets of states and a waiting list $W$ of pairs $(C, b)$ of a set of states $C$ and a letter $b$ satisfy the invariants when: (i) $P$ is a partition of the states into nonempty blocks; (ii) for every $(C, b)$ in $W$, $C$ is an entry of $P$; (iii) for every letter $b$ and all states $p$, $q$ lying in a common entry of $P$, if for every $C$ with…

results.title: One round preserves the invariants
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA, $P$ a list of blocks of states, $W$ a list of pairs of a set of states and a letter, $C$ a set of states and $a$ a letter. If $P$ and the waiting list obtained by putting $(C, a)$ in front of $W$ satisfy the invariants of Hopcroft's loop, then so do the partition after the splitter $(C, a)$ and the waiting list after the splitter $(C, a)$ from the rest $W$.

results.title: With an empty waiting list, blocks are the classes of equal continuation languages
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA and $P$ a list of blocks of states such that $P$ with the empty waiting list satisfies the invariants of Hopcroft's loop. Then two states $p$ and $q$ lie in a common block of $P$ if and only if they accept the same continuation languages, that is, $M$ accepts a word from $p$ exactly when it accepts it from $q$.

results.title: The invariants hold initially
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every DFA $M$ with finitely many states over a finite alphabet, Hopcroft's initial partition and initial waiting list satisfy the invariants of Hopcroft's loop.

results.title: Termination of Hopcroft's loop
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, let $P$ be a partition of the states given as a list of blocks, let $W$ be a waiting list of splitters, and let $k$ be a natural number. If $P$ and $W$ satisfy the invariants of Hopcroft's loop and $|W| + |\Sigma| \cdot (|Q| - |P|) \le k$, where $|P|$ and $|W|$ are the lengths of the lists, then Hopcroft's loop run from $(P, W)$ with a…

results.title: Hopcroft's waiting list is exhausted
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$. Hopcroft's loop, run from the initial partition and the initial waiting list with a budget of $|\Sigma| \cdot (|Q| + 1)$ rounds, ends with an empty waiting list.

results.title: Hopcroft's final partition is a partition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a DFA $M$, Hopcroft's final partition of $M$ is a partition of the states of $M$ into nonempty blocks.

results.title: Correctness of Hopcroft's algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a DFA $M$, two states $p$ and $q$ share a block of Hopcroft's final partition of $M$ exactly when the language accepted by $M$ from $p$ equals the language accepted by $M$ from $q$.

results.title: Hopcroft's partition is Moore's relation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every DFA $M$ with finitely many states over a finite alphabet, Hopcroft's relation of $M$, the set of pairs of states lying in a common block of Hopcroft's partition, equals Moore's state equivalence of $M$ as a set of pairs of states.

results.title: Moore classes are Hopcroft blocks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ and reachable states $p$ and $q$ of $M$, the classes of $p$ and $q$ under Moore's equivalence on reachable states (the states of Moore's minimal automaton) are equal if and only if $p$ and $q$ share a block of Hopcroft's final partition of $M$.

results.title: Blocks of Hopcroft's partition are language classes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA, $D$ a block of Hopcroft's final partition of $M$ and $p$ a state in $D$. Then a state $q$ lies in $D$ if and only if the language accepted by $M$ from $q$ equals the language accepted by $M$ from $p$.

results.title: The smaller of two sets has at most half their total size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The smaller of two sets has at most half their combined size: it is one of the two sets, so twice its size is at most the sum of the two sizes.

results.title: The smaller part of a split has at most half the size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If two disjoint sets union to `D`, the smaller of them has at most half the size of `D`.

results.title: Halving chains shrink blocks by a factor of at least $2^k$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: After `k` halving steps, the initial block is at least `2 ^ k` times the final block. The halving hypothesis is stated for the cardinalities only; no subset hypothesis is needed.

reading_title.source: Halving chains shrink blocks by a factor of at least $2^k$
parts: Halving chains shrink blocks by a factor of at least

results.title: The smaller-half counting lemma
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a chain of blocks where each step at least halves the size, a block containing a given state can occur at most `Nat.log 2 n` times past the start, where `n` is the number of states. In Hopcroft's algorithm, the successive smaller halves containing one fixed state form such a chain: each of them is the smaller half of a split of the previous block containing that state.

results.title: New splitters are halves of the split block
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every entry `newSplitters` adds for a block `D` is a half of `D` (one of the two sides of the split by `pre`), or the smaller half.

results.title: Smaller-half splitters have at most half the block size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A smaller-half entry added by `newSplitters` for a block `D` has at most half the size of `D`: the two halves are disjoint and union to `D`. No split hypothesis is needed: the halves of any block partition it.

results.title: Trace of splitters popped by Hopcroft's algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The splitters popped by Hopcroft's loop, in order: the same recursion as `DFA.hopcroftLoop`, collecting each popped splitter. The cost of processing one popped splitter `(C, a)` is `(preimage M C a).card + 1`: one predecessor visit per state whose `a`-successor lies in `C`, plus `O(1)` per-splitter overhead. See `hopcroftCost`. `hopcroftLoop_eq_hopcroftLoop_of_length` proves this trace records exactly the splitters…

results.title: Predecessor cost of a Hopcroft splitter trace
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The predecessor cost of a splitter trace: for each popped splitter `(C, a)`, one predecessor visit per state in the preimage `preimage M C a`, plus `1` per-splitter overhead. This is the quantity the total-work bound constrains to `O(|Σ| n log n)`. Charging splitter size `C.card` instead would undercount: if all `n` states transition on `a` to one state `q`, processing the singleton splitter `({q}, a)` costs `n`…

results.title: The splitter trace records exactly the splitters the loop pops
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The loop and the trace recurse on the same state, so they take the same number of steps. The two theorems below make the correspondence usable: the trace length is at most `k`, and running the loop for exactly the trace's length gives the full loop result, so the trace contains every splitter the loop pops and no others.

results.title: Hopcroft splitter trace length equals loop fuel
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The trace and the loop take the same number of steps: the trace length is the fuel the loop consumed, i.e. the loop would stop after exactly that many rounds if run with only that much fuel.

results.title: Splitter count of a state and letter
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Number of splitters with letter `b` containing `q`, with multiplicity. This applies both to the waiting list and to the actual popped trace.

results.title: Splitter count of newly added splitters
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Replacement contributes one token at a state in the parent block; otherwise only membership in the smaller half contributes a token.

results.title: Splitter count update after one Hopcroft round
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The exact token update at a state. Only its unique parent block can contribute a new token, even when other blocks split in the same round.

results.title: Waiting entries give positive splitter count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A waiting entry supplies a token; duplicate entries remain counted.

results.title: Refined Hopcroft blocks lie inside their old blocks
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A refined block containing `q` is a subset of the old block containing `q`. Both partitions are the canonical Hopcroft partitions.

results.title: Potential inequality for one Hopcroft refinement round
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: One refinement cannot increase logarithmic block-size credit plus pending-token credit. Replacing a pending splitter spends no new credit; adding a nonpending smaller half spends one logarithmic unit.

results.title: Splitter count bound along a Hopcroft execution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Total state/letter charging along the actual execution. The bound includes initial tokens and tokens still pending through replacements. No amortized bound is assumed in the execution invariant.

results.title: Initial splitter count is at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Initially there is at most one token for each state and letter.

results.title: Hopcroft visits each of $n$ states at most $\log_2 n + 1$ times per letter
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Each state is processed with a fixed letter at most `log₂ n + 1` times during any prefix of the actual initialized Hopcroft execution.

reading_title.source: Hopcroft visits each of $n$ states at most $\log_2 n + 1$ times per letter

results.title: Popped Hopcroft splitters are nonempty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every popped splitter has a nonempty block, including splitters whose predecessor set is empty.

results.title: Hopcroft predecessor-work as splitter counts plus pops
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Double counting visits by source state and letter, retaining every incoming transition even when many sources have the same successor.

results.title: Number of pops bounded by the total splitter count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A nonempty popped block pays for its pop, even if its preimage is empty. This bounds the `+1` term independently of predecessor visits.

results.title: Total predecessor-work bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Total predecessor-work bound, including one unit for every pop, for every prefix of the initialized execution. No runtime claim is made for the scanning implementation or for initialization.

results.title: $O(|\Sigma| n \log n)$ bound on Hopcroft predecessor-work
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A uniform `O(|Σ| n log n)` bound, with the explicit constant `4`. The condition `n ≥ 2` is essential when absorbing the additive unit into the logarithm. This concerns predecessor-work, not scan runtime.

reading_title.source: $O(|\Sigma| n \log n)$ bound on Hopcroft predecessor-work

results.title: Predecessor-work bound for the complete Hopcroft run
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The bound for the complete terminating minimization execution. `DFA.hopcroftLoop_waiting_eq_nil` proves this fuel exhausts the queue; `hopcroftLoop_eq_hopcroftLoop_of_length` ties the trace to its result.

results.title: No initial Hopcroft splitters with at most one state
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With at most one state, the accepting/rejecting split has an empty side, so the algorithm has no initial splitters.

results.title: Zero Hopcroft predecessor-work with at most one state
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Zero predecessor-work for zero/one-state boundary parameters. This does not assert that constructing the initial partition costs zero.

results.title: Zero Hopcroft predecessor-work over an empty alphabet
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An empty alphabet causes no predecessor-work, for any state count.

results.title: Hopcroft loop with recorded predecessor-work
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The actual loop with predecessor-visit and pop events recorded in CSLib's `TimeM`. Pure scans are not charged in this event model.

results.title: Instrumented Hopcroft loop returns the original result
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Instrumentation preserves the exact loop result.

results.title: Recorded Hopcroft cost equals the work of the popped trace
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The recorded cost is exactly the work of the actual popped trace.

results.title: Recorded Hopcroft cost obeys the predecessor-work bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The canonical cost monad records the proved total predecessor-work bound for every initialized execution prefix.

results.title: Instrumented complete Hopcroft run returns the minimization partition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: At the proved terminating fuel, instrumentation returns the original correct minimization partition and an empty waiting list.

path: Lists, stacks, queues and dynamic arrays

results.title: Potential of a two-list queue
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a queue stored as an enqueue list and a dequeue list, the potential is the length of the enqueue list: the number of elements that will be reversed when they are moved to the dequeue list.

results.title: Modeled cost of a dequeue
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a queue stored as an enqueue list and a dequeue list, the modeled cost of dequeueing is $1$ when the dequeue list is nonempty, and $m + 1$ when the dequeue list is empty, where $m$ is the length of the enqueue list (the number of elements reversed when they are moved to the dequeue list).

results.title: Timed enqueue
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Enqueueing a value $v$ onto a two-list queue $q$ returns the queue obtained from $q$ by adding $v$ at the back, that is, by prepending $v$ to the enqueue list, together with a recorded cost of $1$.

results.title: Amortized cost of enqueueing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every two-list queue $q$ and every value $v$, the modeled cost of enqueueing $v$ onto $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus $2$.

results.title: Timed dequeue
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Dequeueing from a two-list queue $q$ returns the next element in first-in, first-out order together with the remaining queue, or returns no element together with $q$ itself when $q$ is empty. In both cases the recorded cost is the modeled dequeue cost of $q$.

results.title: Amortized cost of dequeueing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of dequeueing from $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus $1$. This includes the case where $q$ is empty.

results.title: Queue operation
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A queue operation over a type $\alpha$ is either a request to enqueue a value $v \in \alpha$ or a request to dequeue. Sequences of such operations are used to state aggregate cost bounds.

results.title: Amortized charge of a queue operation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The potential-method charge of a queue operation is $2$ for an enqueue and $1$ for a dequeue.

results.title: One step of a queue operation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a queue $q$, an enqueue operation with value $v$ performs the costed enqueue of $v$ onto $q$. A dequeue operation performs the costed dequeue of $q$ and keeps the remaining queue and the cost, discarding the removed value; on an empty queue the remaining queue is $q$ itself.

results.title: Amortized cost of one queue operation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every queue $q$ and every queue operation $o$, the modeled cost of performing $o$ on $q$ plus the potential of the resulting queue equals the potential of $q$ plus the charge of $o$.

results.title: Running a sequence of queue operations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Running a list of queue operations from a queue $q$ performs the operations one step at a time from left to right, starting at $q$. The result is the final queue, and the cost is the sum of the costs of the individual steps; running the empty list returns $q$ at cost $0$.

results.title: Total charge of a sequence of queue operations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list of queue operations, the total charge is the sum of the amortized charges of its operations, where an enqueue is charged $2$ and a dequeue is charged $1$.

results.title: Amortized cost of a sequence of queue operations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of queue operations and every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of running the operations from left to right starting at $q$, plus the potential of the final queue, equals the potential of $q$ plus the total charge of the operations.

results.title: Linear bound on the cost of queue operations
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of $n$ queue operations and every two-list queue $q$, the modeled cost of running the operations from left to right starting at $q$ is at most the potential of $q$ plus $2n$.

results.title: Contents of a two-list queue
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A queue is stored as a dequeue list and an enqueue list whose most recently enqueued element comes first. Its contents are its elements in FIFO order: the dequeue list followed by the reverse of the enqueue list.

results.title: Array conversion lists the contents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every queue $q$, the array obtained from $q$, read as a list, equals the contents of $q$.

results.title: Enqueueing appends to the contents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every queue $q$ and value $v$, the contents of the queue obtained by enqueueing $v$ onto $q$ are the contents of $q$ followed by $v$.

results.title: The queue emptiness test matches the contents
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every queue $q$, the emptiness test of $q$ returns true if and only if the contents of $q$ are empty.

results.title: Dequeueing fails exactly on empty queues
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every queue $q$, dequeueing $q$ returns nothing if and only if the contents of $q$ are empty.

results.title: A successful dequeue splits off the first element
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If dequeueing a queue $q$ succeeds and returns an element $a$ and a queue $r$, then the contents of $q$ are $a$ followed by the contents of $r$.

results.title: Rooted weak transition
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a labelled transition system whose labels include a silent label $\tau$, there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$ when there are states $s_1$ and $s_2$ such that $s$ reaches $s_1$ by zero or more $\tau$-transitions, $s_1 \xrightarrow{\mu} s_2$ is a transition, and $s_2$ reaches $t$ by zero or more $\tau$-transitions. In particular, a rooted weak transition with label $\tau$ contains at…

results.title: Transitions are rooted weak transitions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, every transition $s \xrightarrow{\mu} t$ is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$.

results.title: Rooted weak transitions are weak transitions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, every rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$ is a weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$, where a weak transition with label $\mu$ is either the trivial step from a state to itself with label $\tau$, or a transition with label $\mu$ preceded and followed by zero or more $\tau$-transitions.

results.title: Silent steps before a rooted weak transition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, if $s$ reaches $m$ by zero or more $\tau$-transitions and there is a rooted weak transition from $m$ to $t$ with label $\mu$, then there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$.

results.title: Appending silent steps to a rooted weak transition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with silent action $\tau$, if there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $m$ with label $a$, and $t$ is reachable from $m$ by zero or more $\tau$-transitions, then there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $a$.

results.title: A rooted silent step followed by a weak transition is rooted
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, if there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $m$ with label $\tau$ and a weak transition from $m$ to $t$ with label $\mu$, then there is a rooted weak transition from $s$ to $t$ with label $\mu$. Here a weak transition with label $\mu$ is either the trivial step from a state to itself with label $\tau$, or a transition with label $\mu$ preceded and…

results.title: Rooted observation congruence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, states $p$ and $q$ are rooted weakly bisimilar (observation congruent) when every transition $p \xrightarrow{\mu} p'$ is matched by a rooted weak transition from $q$ to some $q'$ with label $\mu$ such that $p'$ and $q'$ are weakly bisimilar, and every transition $q \xrightarrow{\mu} q'$ is matched by a rooted weak transition from $p$ to some $p'$ with…

results.title: Observation congruence matches rooted weak transitions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, if $p$ and $q$ are rooted weakly bisimilar and there is a rooted weak transition from $p$ to $p'$ with label $\mu$, then there is a state $q'$ with a rooted weak transition from $q$ to $q'$ with label $\mu$ such that $p'$ and $q'$ are weakly bisimilar.

results.title: Transitivity of rooted observational congruence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with silent action $\tau$, if $p$ is rooted observationally congruent to $q$ and $q$ is rooted observationally congruent to $r$, then $p$ is rooted observationally congruent to $r$.

results.title: Observation congruence is an equivalence relation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In every labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, rooted weak bisimilarity (observation congruence) is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

results.title: Strong bisimilarity implies observation congruence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, any two strongly bisimilar states are rooted weakly bisimilar.

results.title: Observation congruence implies weak bisimilarity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a labelled transition system with a silent label $\tau$, any two rooted weakly bisimilar states are weakly bisimilar.

path: One-time pad over a finite group

results.title: The group one-time pad
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group. The group one-time pad on $G$ is the private-key encryption scheme with messages, keys and ciphertexts in $G$ whose key $k$ is drawn uniformly from $G$, which encrypts a message $m$ as $k m$, and which decrypts a ciphertext $c$ as $k^{-1} c$.

results.title: Group one-time pad ciphertexts are uniform
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group. For every message $m \in G$, the ciphertext of $m$ under the group one-time pad on $G$, whose key is drawn uniformly from $G$, is uniformly distributed on $G$.

results.title: The group one-time pad is perfectly secret
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group. The group one-time pad on $G$ is perfectly secret: for every probability distribution on messages in $G$ and every ciphertext $c$ that occurs with positive probability, the conditional distribution of the message given that the ciphertext is $c$ equals the prior distribution of the message.

part.title: Profile scores for amino acid substitutions

path: Profile scores for amino acid substitutions

results.title: Profile log-odds score of a residue
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The profile log-odds score `log (p a / q a)` of residue `a`: `p` is the position-specific profile probability (estimated from aligned homologs), `q` the background probability. Meaningful for `p a, q a > 0`; otherwise Lean's `log 0 = 0` and `x / 0 = 0` give junk.

results.title: The score is a log-likelihood ratio
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a sequence `s` over independent positions with profiles `p j` and background `q` (all positive), the summed profile score is the log of the likelihood ratio `∏ p_j(s_j) / ∏ q(s_j)` of the profile model against the background.

results.title: Gibbs' inequality for the profile score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `p` and `q` are probability vectors and `q` is positive, the expected score under the profile, `∑ p a log (p a / q a)` (the Kullback–Leibler divergence), is nonnegative.

results.title: Expected profile score under the background is nonpositive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `p` and `q` are probability vectors and `p` is positive, the expected score under the background, `∑ q a log (p a / q a)`, is nonpositive.

results.title: PSIC score difference of a substitution
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The PSIC score difference of a substitution from the wild-type residue `wt` to the mutant residue `mt`: `profileScore p q wt - profileScore p q mt`.

results.title: PSIC difference as a log ratio of likelihood ratios
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The PSIC difference is the log of the ratio of the two residues' likelihood ratios.

results.title: Positivity criterion for the PSIC difference
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The PSIC difference is positive iff the wild type is more enriched in the profile, relative to background, than the mutant.

results.title: Two-class naive Bayes model
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A two-class naive Bayes model: class *damaging* has prior `prior ∈ (0, 1)`, class *benign* the complement; each feature `j` takes values in the finite type `X j` with class-conditional probabilities `damaging j` and `benign j`, assumed positive; features are conditionally independent given the class. The tables are estimated from training data.

results.title: Joint probability of class and features in naive Bayes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The joint probability of class `c` (`true` = damaging) and feature values `x`: `π ∏ P_D(x_j)` or `(1 - π) ∏ P_B(x_j)`.

results.title: Naive Bayes joint law is a probability law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The joint law of class and features is a probability law.

results.title: Naive Bayes posterior probability of damage
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The posterior probability that the variant is damaging given feature values `x` (Bayes' rule on the joint law).

results.title: Log-likelihood ratio of a feature value
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The log-likelihood ratio `log (P_D(v) / P_B(v))` of value `v` of feature `j`.

results.title: Naive Bayes score
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The naive-Bayes score: prior log-odds plus the features' log-likelihood ratios.

results.title: Naive-Bayes posterior
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The posterior probability of *damaging* is the logistic function of the score.

results.title: Naive Bayes posterior is strictly monotone in the score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The posterior is strictly monotone in the score.

results.title: Monotonicity in a feature value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let feature `j` carry a numerical value `g v` (for example a PSIC-difference bin) such that its likelihood ratio `P_D(v) / P_B(v)` is monotone in `g v`. With the other features fixed, the posterior is monotone in `g`.

outside: The logistic function of the log odds

uses: Tumour purity, ploidy and copy-ratio algebra

results.title: Posterior tail probability on a grid
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Posterior probability that the parameter `c i` exceeds `t`, for prior weights `prior` and likelihoods `lik i` of the observed data: `∑_{c i > t} prior i lik i / ∑_i prior i lik i`.

results.title: Monotone likelihood ratio implies stochastically larger posteriors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the kernels `L` (data `x`) and `L'` (data `x'`) satisfy the TP2 inequality `L' i L j ≥ L i L' j` whenever `c j ≤ c i`, then for a nonnegative prior every posterior tail `P(c > t)` is at least as large under `L'` as under `L` (both normalizers positive).

results.title: The binomial family is TP2
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The binomial family is TP2 (monotone likelihood ratio in the success probability): for `a ≤ a'` and `0 ≤ p ≤ p' ≤ 1`, `Binom(a | n, p') Binom(a' | n, p) ≤ Binom(a' | n, p') Binom(a | n, p)`.

results.title: Posterior probability that the cancer cell fraction exceeds a threshold
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Landau et al.'s posterior probability that the CCF exceeds `t`, given `a` of `n` reads, purity `α`, copy number `q`, a prior `prior` on the grid points `grid k`: `∑_{grid k > t} π_k Binom(a | n, f(grid k)) / ∑_k π_k Binom(a | n, f(grid k))`, with `f(c) = α c / (α q + 2 (1 - α))`.

results.title: Clonal call for a mutation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Landau et al.'s clonal call: `P(CCF > t | a) > γ` (they take `t = 0.95`, `γ = 0.5`).

results.title: Grid model for the cancer cell fraction
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Hypotheses on the CCF grid model: purity `0 < α ≤ 1`, copy number `q > 0`, grid in `[0, q]` and within the defining CCF bound `≤ 1`, a nonnegative prior, and one grid point of positive prior weight whose allelic fraction lies strictly inside `(0, 1)` (this makes every posterior well defined).

results.title: Positivity of the grid posterior normalizer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In a grid model every posterior normalizer `∑_k π_k Binom(a | n, f(grid k))`, `a ≤ n`, is positive.

results.title: The CCF posterior is stochastically increasing in the read count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The CCF posterior is stochastically increasing in the read count (Landau et al. 2013 with the monotone-likelihood-ratio argument): `P(CCF > t | a) ≤ P(CCF > t | a')` for `a ≤ a' ≤ n`.

results.title: The clonal call is upward closed in the read count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The clonal call is upward closed in the read count.

results.title: The clonal call is a read-count threshold
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every CCF threshold `t` and posterior level `γ` there is `a₀` such that, for `a ≤ n`, the mutation is called clonal iff `a₀ ≤ a` (`a₀ = n + 1` when no count is called clonal).

results.title: Maximum-likelihood cancer cell fraction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The continuous maximum-likelihood CCF `ĉ = min 1 (a / (n κ))` for the allelic-fraction slope `κ = α / (α q + 2 (1 - α))`. Landau et al. (2013) use the grid posterior; this continuous maximizer over `[0, 1]` is derived here.

results.title: The continuous CCF MLE
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `0 < α ≤ 1`, `q ≥ 1`, `a ≤ n` and `0 < n`, the likelihood `c ↦ Binom(a | n, f(c))` on `[0, 1]` is maximized at `ĉ = min 1 (a / (n κ))`.
